### Problem: Honest Coach {#sec-srt-p1-b}

::: {.p-statement}

Each test case gives $n$ athletes ($2 \le n \le 50$) with strengths $s_1, \dots, s_n$ ($1 \le s_i \le 1000$). Split them into **two non-empty teams** $A$ and $B$ so that the value $|\max(A) - \min(B)|$ is as small as possible — the coach wants the strongest athlete of one team to be as close as possible to the weakest of the other. Print that minimum value. The first input line is $t$ ($1 \le t \le 1000$), the number of test cases.

Source: [CF 1360B · Honest Coach](https://codeforces.com/problemset/problem/1360/B){.solved rating="800"}

Example — one test case: $n = 5$, $s = [3, 1, 2, 6, 4]$. Output $1$ (put $[1,2,3]$ in one team and $[4,6]$ in the other: the seam is $|3 - 4| = 1$).
:::

::: {.p-intuition}
The seam $|\max(A) - \min(B)|$ is realised by **two athletes sitting next to each other in the sorted order.** Sort the strengths. Two facts finish it. Any split gives $|\max(A) - \min(B)|$ equal to the difference of two different athletes, so it is at least the smallest difference between any two athletes, which is the smallest adjacent gap $g$ of the sorted array. And cutting the sorted array at that gap (left part to $A$, right part to $B$) achieves exactly $g$. So the answer is the smallest adjacent gap. This is the very same "sort, then scan neighbours" move as @sec-srt-p1-a, wearing a story about teams instead of pairs.
:::

::: {.p-approach}
1. **Try every pair.** For each $i < j$ record $|s_i - s_j|$ and keep the minimum. That minimum is a lower bound on every split's seam (a seam is always the difference of two athletes), and the closest pair is achievable (see the invariant). $O(n^2)$ time — the oracle.
2. **Insertion sort, then take the smallest adjacent gap.** Buy sortedness with the hand-written $O(n^2)$ insertion sort, then run the same $n-1$ neighbour scan. Same asymptotic time as the pair scan in the worst case, but the two ideas (sorting, adjacent gap) are separated so you can see which half the pattern actually uses.
3. **Sort, then take the smallest adjacent gap.** Sort with the built-in; answer $= \min_i (s[i+1] - s[i])$. $O(n\log n)$ time.

**Invariant.** Lower bound: for any split, $|\max(A) - \min(B)|$ is $|s_i - s_j|$ for two different athletes, so it is $\ge$ the smallest pair difference, which equals the smallest adjacent gap of the sorted array (@sec-srt-p1-a). Achievability: if that gap sits between $b_k$ and $b_{k+1}$, put $b_0 \dots b_k$ in $A$ and the rest in $B$; then $\max(A) = b_k$ and $\min(B) = b_{k+1}$. So answer $= \min$ adjacent gap.
:::

The buttons are in order. Each one keeps the previous solution and changes only what that form changes.

::: {.panel-tabset .solution-forms}

#### Try every pair

::: {.form-next}
The closest two athletes anywhere are the best seam, so scan all $\binom{n}{2}$ unordered pairs and keep the smallest absolute difference. $O(n^2)$ time, $O(1)$ space — per test case with $n \le 50$ this is instant, and it is exactly the "closest pair" oracle from @sec-srt-p1-a in a different costume.

**Worked example.** $s = [3, 1, 2, 6, 4]$. Pairwise differences include $|3-2|=1$, $|1-2|=1$, $|6-4|=2$, $|3-4|=1$, and the smallest overall is $1$. So the answer is $1$ — the split that puts, say, $\{1,2,3\}$ and $\{4,6\}$ on either side of the $3|4$ seam.
:::

```{python}

    assert str(final) == "1"

V.show(draw)
```

::: {.panel-tabset group="lang"}
##### Python

```{python}
def honest_brute(s):
    best = math.inf
    n = len(s)
    for i in range(n):
        for j in range(i + 1, n):
            best = min(best, abs(s[i] - s[j]))
    return best
```

##### C++

```cpp
// fragment - brute force oracle
#include <vector>
#include <algorithm>
#include <climits>
using namespace std;
int honestBrute(const vector<int>& s) {
    int best = INT_MAX, n = (int)s.size();
    for (int i = 0; i < n; ++i)
        for (int j = i + 1; j < n; ++j)
            best = min(best, abs(s[i] - s[j]));
    return best;
}
```
:::

**Reading it line by line.** The double loop names every unordered pair once; `best = min(best, abs(s[i] - s[j]))` keeps the closest pair. That is the answer because every seam is some pair's difference and the closest pair can be made the seam (the invariant above). The stress test in the last form also checks this against an enumeration of every split.

#### Insertion sort, then take the smallest adjacent gap

::: {.form-next}
The pattern is *sort then scan*, so let's earn the sort by hand before we outsource it. $O(n^2)$ insertion sort (worst case; $O(n)$ if the strengths are already nearly sorted), then one linear pass over the $n-1$ adjacent gaps. Same asymptotic ceiling as the pair scan, but the work splits cleanly: the sortedness step is reusable across every other problem in this chapter, and only the seam scan is new here.

**Insertion sort, in plain words.** Walk left to right; sink each new element toward the front by swapping it with its left neighbour while that neighbour is bigger. After pass $i$, positions $0..i$ are sorted.

**Worked example.** $s = [3, 1, 2, 6, 4]$. Pass 1 sinks $1$ past $3$: $[1, 3, 2, 6, 4]$. Pass 2 sinks $2$ past $3$: $[1, 2, 3, 6, 4]$. Pass 3 keeps $6$ in place: $[1, 2, 3, 6, 4]$. Pass 4 sinks $4$ past $6$: $[1, 2, 3, 4, 6]$. Adjacent gaps $1, 1, 1, 2$, minimum $1$ — matches the pair scan and the sample output.
:::


::: {.panel-tabset group="lang"}
##### Python

```{python}
#| label: arr-1360b-ins
def honest_ins(s):
    b = list(s)
    for i in range(1, len(b)):
        j = i
        while j > 0 and b[j - 1] > b[j]:
            b[j - 1], b[j] = b[j], b[j - 1]
            j -= 1
    return min(b[i + 1] - b[i] for i in range(len(b) - 1))

for _ in range(300):
    s = [random.randint(1, 1000) for _ in range(random.randint(2, 12))]
    assert honest_ins(s) == honest_brute(s)
assert honest_ins([3, 1, 2, 6, 4]) == 1
assert honest_ins([2, 1, 3, 2, 4, 3]) == 0
print("honest_ins OK")
```

##### C++

```cpp
#include <vector>
#include <algorithm>
#include <climits>
using namespace std;

int honestCoachIns(vector<int> b) {
    int n = (int)b.size();
    for (int i = 1; i < n; ++i) {
        int j = i;
        while (j > 0 && b[j - 1] > b[j]) {
            std::swap(b[j - 1], b[j]);
            --j;
        }
    }
    int best = INT_MAX;
    for (int i = 1; i < n; ++i) best = min(best, b[i] - b[i - 1]);
    return best;
}

int main() { vector<int> v{3, 1, 2, 6, 4}; honestCoachIns(v); }
```
:::

**Reading it line by line.** The `while j > 0 and b[j-1] > b[j]` loop is the textbook insertion-sort step; after $n-1$ passes, `b` is sorted and the seam scan takes over. The last line `min(b[i+1] - b[i] ...)` is *literally the same expression* as in the optimal form below — the only difference is that here we paid $O(n^2)$ to obtain `b`, and there the language's sort gives it to us for $O(n\log n)$.

#### Sort with the built-in, then take the smallest adjacent gap

::: {.form-next}
Sort once with `sorted()` / `std::sort` and the tightest seam is a *neighbour* gap. $O(n\log n)$ time. Where the brute checks every pair and the middle rung pays $O(n^2)$ to build the order by hand, the built-in sort hands us the same order for $O(n\log n)$ and the seam scan is unchanged.

**Worked example.** $s = [3, 1, 2, 6, 4]$ sorted to $[1, 2, 3, 4, 6]$. Adjacent gaps: $1, 1, 1, 2$. The minimum is $1$, matching both the pair scan and the insertion-sort rung — and cutting the sorted list at any of the three unit gaps gives a valid two-team split with seam $1$.
:::

```{python}

    V.story(ax, p, title, inp, steps, final)
V.show(draw)
```

::: {.panel-tabset group="lang"}
##### Python

```{python}
#| label: arr-1360b-scan
def honest_scan(s):
    b = sorted(s)
    return min(b[i + 1] - b[i] for i in range(len(b) - 1))

def honest_splits(s):                              # the statement: try every split
    n, best = len(s), math.inf
    for mask in range(1, (1 << n) - 1):            # both teams non-empty
        A = [s[i] for i in range(n) if mask >> i & 1]
        B = [s[i] for i in range(n) if not mask >> i & 1]
        best = min(best, abs(max(A) - min(B)))
    return best

for _ in range(300):
    s = [random.randint(1, 1000) for _ in range(random.randint(2, 12))]
    assert honest_scan(s) == honest_brute(s)
for _ in range(200):
    s = [random.randint(1, 20) for _ in range(random.randint(2, 8))]
    assert honest_scan(s) == honest_splits(s)
assert honest_scan([3, 1, 2, 6, 4]) == 1          # sample test case; the board sample
assert honest_scan([2, 1, 3, 2, 4, 3]) == 0        # duplicate strengths -> seam 0
assert honest_scan([7, 9, 3, 1]) == 2
assert honest_scan([1, 1000]) == 999
assert honest_scan([100, 150, 200]) == 50
print("honest_scan OK")
```

##### C++

```cpp
#include <vector>
#include <algorithm>
#include <climits>
#include <iostream>
using namespace std;

int honestCoach(vector<int> s) {
    sort(s.begin(), s.end());
    int best = INT_MAX;
    for (int i = 1; i < (int)s.size(); ++i) best = min(best, s[i] - s[i - 1]);
    return best;
}

int main() {
    ios::sync_with_stdio(false); cin.tie(nullptr);
    int t; cin >> t;
    while (t--) {
        int n; cin >> n;
        vector<int> s(n);
        for (int& x : s) cin >> x;
        cout << honestCoach(s) << '\n';
    }
}
```
:::

**Reading it line by line.** `b = sorted(s)` is the one-time sort. `min(b[i + 1] - b[i] ...)` walks the $n-1$ adjacent gaps; sortedness makes every difference non-negative (no `abs` needed) and — by the "closest pair is adjacent" lemma — guarantees the smallest gap here is the global smallest difference. Duplicate strengths give a $0$ gap, which is a legal answer (two equal athletes on either side of the seam). The `main` reads $t$ test cases and prints one line each — the multi-case shell every Codeforces problem wraps around the real algorithm.
:::

::: {.p-complexity}
**Try every pair** is $O(n^2)$ time, $O(1)$ space. **Insertion sort + seam scan** is $O(n^2)$ worst case, $O(n)$ best case, $O(1)$ extra space beyond the array — same asymptotic ceiling as the pair scan, but the sort is now a reusable asset. **Built-in sort + seam scan** is $O(n\log n)$ time, $O(1)$ extra space (in-place). With $n \le 50$ any of the three passes instantly; the point is not the constant but the *idea* — the same reduction that turns LC 1200 linear also settles this, which is why the two problems share one pattern.
:::

::: {.p-edge}
- Duplicates: if two athletes share a strength the answer is $0$ (put them on opposite teams at the seam) — the adjacent scan sees the $0$ gap directly.
- $n = 2$: one pair, answer $|s_0 - s_1|$; both forms agree.
- Non-empty teams: the cut is between adjacent elements, so neither side is ever empty.
:::

::: {.practice}
- [CF 1607C · Minimum Extraction](https://codeforces.com/problemset/problem/1607/C){rating="1000"} — sort, and the answer is the largest of the first element and the adjacent gaps.
- [CF 1360C · Similar Pairs](https://codeforces.com/problemset/problem/1360/C){rating="1100"} — parity counting, with a sorted adjacent pair at distance $1$ as the escape hatch.
:::
